content.body: Welcome! Today we'll solve a classic problem: finding the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray. This is called the Maximum Subarray problem, and we'll learn Kadane's Algorithm to solve it efficiently. By the end, you'll be able to find the best segment of numbers in any array.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply Kadane's Algorithm to find maximum subarray sums.
• Implement the algorithm using a single pass through the array.
• Explain why tracking current and global maxima is efficient.
• Recognize when this approach beats checking every possible subarray.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a small example. Look at this array:
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: What's the maximum sum you can get from any contiguous block of numbers?
content.successMessage: Nice! The subarray [3] gives sum 3, which is the maximum.

content.title: Try a bigger array
content.prompt: Now try this array. What's the maximum contiguous sum?
content.successMessage: Well done! The subarray [4, -1, 2, 1] gives sum 6.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: Last one. Find the maximum contiguous sum here:
content.successMessage: Great! The whole array [5, 4, -1, 7, 8] gives sum 23.

content.body: What you just did was examine different segments manually. For small arrays, you might check every possible subarray. That's the brute force approach—it works but becomes very slow as arrays grow.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the array has 10,000 numbers, checking every possible subarray means checking millions of combinations. That's too slow for real applications. We need a smarter method that finds the answer in one pass. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. Instead of checking all subarrays, we can track the best sum ending at each position as we move through the array. Show the learner how to use a lookup structure (like variables) to remember the best sums we've computed so far and avoid re-scanning.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like keeping a notebook where we write down the best running total we've seen so far, and update it at each step.

content.body: We'll use Kadane's Algorithm. It works by maintaining two variables: one tracks the maximum sum of subarrays ending at the current position, and another tracks the global maximum seen so far.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1]:
Start: currentMax = -2, globalMax = -2
At 1: currentMax = max(1, -2+1) = 1, globalMax = 1
At -3: currentMax = max(-3, 1-3) = -2, globalMax = 1
At 4: currentMax = max(4, -2+4) = 4, globalMax = 4
At -1: currentMax = max(-1, 4-1) = 3, globalMax = 4
At 2: currentMax = max(2, 3+2) = 5, globalMax = 5
At 1: currentMax = max(1, 5+1) = 6, globalMax = 6
Result: 6

content.body:
1. Initialize two variables: currentMax and globalMax, both set to the first element.
2. Loop through the rest of the array.
3. For each number, update currentMax to be the maximum of the number itself or currentMax + number.
4. Update globalMax to be the maximum of globalMax and currentMax.
5. After the loop, globalMax holds the answer.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function named maxSubArray that takes an array nums as a parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've defined the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure the function takes nums as a parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's start with the basic function definition.

steps.title: Initialize variables
steps.instruction: Inside the function, initialize currentMax and globalMax variables. Both should start as the first element of nums.
steps.hint: Use let to declare variables and set them to nums[0].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the initial tracking variables.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check that both variables are initialized to nums[0].
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to create currentMax and globalMax, both starting with the first array element.

steps.title: Implement the loop
steps.instruction: Add a for loop that goes from the second element to the end. Inside, update currentMax as the maximum of the current number or currentMax + number. Then update globalMax as the maximum of itself and currentMax. Finally, return globalMax.
steps.hint: Use Math.max for comparisons and return globalMax after the loop.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've implemented Kadane's Algorithm correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your loop start index and the Math.max calls.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's walk through it: loop from i=1, update currentMax and globalMax using Math.max, then return globalMax.

content.body: Congratulations! You've learned and implemented Kadane's Algorithm for the Maximum Subarray problem. Remember: we track the best sum ending at each position (currentMax) and the overall best (globalMax). This single-pass approach is much faster than checking all subarrays. Keep practicing with different arrays to solidify your understanding!
